title: Upcoming Events!
subtitle: The Frontier Psychiatrists are venturing, again, into the real world.
body_html:
Oh, my good golly gosh! It’s time to tell the world! Hot on the heels of 2024’s excellent live-action newsletter events, which we called Rapid Acting Mental Health Treatment, Today we announce virtual events and more in-person events!

RAMHT—co-founded with Grady Hannah—continues this year in SF on January 12th, 2025. It will feature more fast-paced conversations about the future of things that work quickly to alleviate suffering. More on that soon, but the tickets are available now! That one is in-person.

RAMHT Tickets!

We also have two events co-created with my dear friend Kari Groff, M.D., of the Brooklyn and Beyond Mental Health Group Community. She saw the need for classes for health professionals on interacting with insurance.

The first will focus on in-network providers on December 4th, on Zoom at 11 am.

Health Insurance Masterclass: I

The second will focus on out-of-network providers, December 9th, on Zoom, at 11 am.

Health Insurance Masterclass: II

These are interactive workshops that are designed to be fun, casual, and answer your questions that you can't ask anywhere else. We're going to review the history and some of the economic rationale behind why insurance works the way it does, and then provide concrete answers to your questions along with proven tips and tricks to navigate the system just a little bit better.

Thank you for reading the newsletter, as always, and I look forward to seeing you either in person or online at the above events!

This was not really a great read, and I know that, because not everything's gonna be magic. I'm gonna get back to writing a really exciting article about the data on GLP-1s in addiction— because there's more of it now.

To make this not a total loss for anyone who just wants to read a newsletter and not have events marketed at them, I will provide the following scene from a book I’m working on.

“There are hedgehog antipsychotics,” I add, trying to be helpful.

“You know what they give to dogs?” asked Carlene.

“What?” I asked.

“Ketamine,” she answers,

“Do they?” I say absentmindedly.

“Oh, yeah. I mean, it is a veterinary anesthetic,” Carlene reminds me.

“It's a veterinary anesthetic.” I agree.

“If it helps humans with depression, and this dog is depressed, then maybe it should have it,” she adds.

“But really, this is more of a trauma situation. We need the MDMA with assisted petting therapy.  We can call it MDMA-AP,” I reply.

“Didn't Dr. Rick Doblin propose MDMA for dogs?” Carlene asks.

“Maybe? I was just joking,” I respond.

“I mean, you were, but we were told that by someone in the space. They were looking into a research trial on MDMA-assisted dog …petting.”

“Doesn't the FDA regulate drugs for dogs, too? Probably, right? Yes, it's like pharmacists. Yeah, they're dog pharmacists. They're going to run into the same challenges.  I mean, Blind? I mean, how do you assess the patient-rated outcome measures? Canine-rated outcome measures. CROMs.  Get some CROMs on these pups.”

“I think the therapy that Lykos proposed would be appropriate for dogs. They love the petting--Therapeutic touch,” I reply.

“They love petting,” Carlene agrees.

“They don't have much more than inner healing intelligence to work with,” I hazard.

“Poodles are very intelligent already, but some other dogs are pretty…stupid. They need to get in touch with their inner healing intelligence. Inner puppy intelligence?” the wheels were spinning in Carlene’s head.

“It is hard when you don't believe you're a good dog,” I countered, continuing, “You hear “good dog,” and that becomes invalidating in the context of trauma.”

“Maybe they've come to believe they're bad dogs?” Carlene replied.

“What they need is an integration walk in which they're told they're a good dog, when they're more open to hearing how good of a dog they are, thanks to the medicine, which could be chicken flavored,” I continued.

“Let's hope nobody there is…well, you know,” Carlene added.  There was a longer pause than I had expected.

“A puppy killer,” she concluded.
